stemMd: In the 1920s Le Corbusier summed up his idea of modern architecture in 'five points', which the Villa Savoye at Poissy, completed in 1931, puts into practice. Which of the following is **not** one of the five points?

options.label: A
options.textMd: Long horizontal windows running across the facade

options.label: B
options.textMd: A free plan, with interior walls placed independently of the structure

options.label: C
options.textMd: Thick load-bearing outer walls that carry the floors

options.label: D
options.textMd: A garden laid out on the flat roof

options.label: E
options.textMd: Pilotis: slender columns that lift the building off the ground

explanationMd:
**What to notice first.** All five points follow from one structural idea: a reinforced-concrete frame of columns and floor slabs carries the whole building. Once the walls carry nothing, they can be moved, opened up or left out wherever the architect likes.

**The fact that settles it.** Le Corbusier's five points are: pilotis, the roof garden, the free plan, the long horizontal window, and the free facade. The free facade means that the outer wall is a light skin hung on the frame rather than a support. Thick load-bearing outer walls are exactly what that point abolishes - they belong to the masonry tradition the five points were written against.

**How to check it.** Walk round the Villa Savoye in your mind. The main floor is raised on slender pilotis; a roof garden and terraces sit on top; the interior is arranged freely around a ramp; and continuous strip windows wrap all four sides. Windows that run the full length of a wall are possible only because the concrete frame, not the wall, carries the floors.

distractorRationale.e: Pilotis can look like a mere engineering detail rather than a design principle, but they are the first of the five points: raising the building frees the ground beneath it. At the Villa Savoye the main floor sits above a recessed ground floor on slender columns.
distractorRationale.d: A roof garden can seem a decorative extra, but it is one of the five points: a flat roof, made possible by the concrete slab, gives back as garden the ground that the building occupies.
distractorRationale.b: The free plan can be mistaken for a matter of interior decoration, but it is one of the five points and follows directly from the frame: since columns carry the floors, partition walls can go wherever the plan needs them.
distractorRationale.a: Traditional facades have tall, vertical windows, so a horizontal window can seem an odd choice for a principle. It is nonetheless one of the five points - the fenetre en longueur - and it depends on the facade carrying no load.

accessibilityText: Question: in the 1920s Le Corbusier summed up modern architecture in five points, put into practice at the Villa Savoye at Poissy, completed in 1931. Which of the following is not one of the five points? The choices are: long horizontal windows running across the facade; a free plan, with interior walls placed independently of the structure; thick load-bearing outer walls that carry the floors; a garden laid out on the flat roof; and pilotis, slender columns that lift the building off the ground.

provenance.notes: Original item written for this bank for the TIL-A History and general knowledge section. Four choices are genuine points (pilotis, roof garden, free plan, horizontal window); the remaining choice, load-bearing outer walls, is the opposite of the point left out of the list, the free facade, so exactly one choice is not a point.

review.author: wave6-polito-til-a-genknow-author

independentSolve.workingNotes: Le Corbusier's five points are pilotis, free plan, free facade, ribbon (horizontal) windows and roof garden. A, B, D and E are all on that list. Thick load-bearing outer walls are exactly what the free plan and free facade reject. [A second, separate blind solve (blind-reviewer-wave7-tila-reading-gk-run1) reached the same answer: Le Corbusier's five points are pilotis, free plan, free facade, ribbon (horizontal) windows and roof garden. A, B, D and E are four of them. Thick load-bearing outer walls are the opposite of the free plan and free facade, so C is the one that is not a point.]

review.notes: Author's uniqueness check: the five points are pilotis, roof garden, free plan, horizontal window and free facade. Four of the choices name four of them; the load-bearing outer wall contradicts the free facade and is the only choice that is not a point. Awaiting a blind independent solve before publication.
